claims.claim: Replaced token detection: a new, more sample-efficient pre-training task in which a discriminator predicts, for every input token, whether a small generator replaced it
claims.quote: As an alternative, we propose a more sample-efficient pre-training task called replaced token detection.
claims.ablation_quote: To provide a fair comparison, we also train a BERT-Small model using the same hyperparameters.

claims.claim: Learning from all input tokens rather than the masked subset makes the task more compute-efficient than MLM
claims.quote: A key advantage of our discriminative task is that the model learns from all input tokens instead of just the small masked-out subset, making it more computationally efficient.
claims.ablation_quote: First, we find that ELECTRA is greatly benefiting from having a loss defined over all input tokens rather than just a subset: ELECTRA 15% performs much worse than ELECTRA.

claims.claim: ELECTRA-Small can be trained on one GPU in 4 days and outperforms GPT on GLUE
claims.quote: we train a model on one GPU for 4 days that outperforms GPT (trained using 30x more compute) on the GLUE natural lan-

claims.claim: At large scale ELECTRA matches RoBERTa/XLNet with under 1/4 of their compute, beats them at equal compute, and sets a new SQuAD 2.0 state of the art
claims.quote: and sets a new state-of-the-art for SQuAD 2.0.

claims.claim: Sharing embeddings between the generator and discriminator (proposed model extension)
claims.quote: We propose improving the efficiency of the pre-training by sharing weights be- tween the generator and discriminator.
claims.ablation_quote: GLUE scores are 83.6 for no weight tying, 84.3 for tying token embeddings, and 84.4 for tying all weights.

claims.claim: Using a smaller generator (1/4 to 1/2 the size of the discriminator) works best
claims.quote: Nevertheless, we find that models work best with generators 1/4-1/2 the size of the discriminator.
claims.ablation_quote: GLUE scores for differently-sized generators and discriminators are shown in the left of Figure 3. All models are trained for 500k steps,

claims.claim: Joint maximum-likelihood training of the generator works better than two-stage or adversarial training
claims.quote: Although still outperforming BERT, we found adversarial training to underperform maximum-likelihood training.
claims.ablation_quote: During two-stage training, downstream task performance notably improves after the switch from the generative to the discriminative objective, but does not end up outscoring joint training.

seeds.quote: We therefore report the median of 10 fine-tuning runs from the same pre-trained checkpoint for each result.

rerun.quote: As a baseline, we trained our own BERT-Large model using the same hyperparameters and training time as ELECTRA-400K.

scores_copied.quote: BERT dev results are from Clark et al. (2019).

third_party.quote: we report the average score excluding QNLI (Avg.*) in addition to the GLUE leaderboard score (Score).

data_disclosure.quote: which extends the BERT dataset to 33B tokens by including data from ClueWeb (Callan et al., 2009), CommonCrawl, and Gigaword (Parker et al., 2011).

tokens_disclosed.quote: For most experiments we pre-train on the same data as BERT, which consists of 3.3 Billion tokens from Wikipedia and BooksCorpus

coding.note: The ablations are matched comparisons in GLUE dev scores (Table 1 BERT-Small vs ELECTRA-Small, Table 5 stepping stones, and the weight-tying numbers). The generator-size ablation is shown only in a figure, but the settings are matched (500k steps), so I coded it YES. The training-algorithm comparison appears only as curves in a figure, so it is PARTIAL. Seeds: 10 fine-tuning runs from one pre-trained checkpoint, reported as a median with no variance, so MULTI rather than VAR. There is only one pre-training run per model. Tokens: the paper gives dataset sizes (3.3B and 33B tokens) plus steps and batch size, but not the total number of tokens trained on, so the Y is borderline. Third party: I coded YES because of the GLUE leaderboard and SQuAD 2.0 test-server results. Renames: the paper says ELECTRA 'can be viewed as a massively scaled-up version of' CBOW with negative sampling and is related to NCE. However, it presents replaced token detection as new, with a learned generator and a Transformer, not as a renaming, so I listed no renames. Data: the sources are named but no mixture proportions are given, so PARTIAL.
